screens.title: BGP Route Manipulation and Path Control
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to shape traffic at the BGP layer by changing path attributes. These attributes let you influence the BGP best path algorithm so your network sends or receives traffic where you intend. We will cover four primary knobs — WEIGHT for router-local decisions; LOCAL_PREF for AS-wide outbound preference; AS_PATH prepending to discourage external peers; and MED to hint preferred entry points for an adjacent AS. You'll also learn how to implement these changes safely with route-maps and prefix-lists, how to apply them in the correct direction, and how to verify results with show commands. Practical examples and a step-by-step lab will walk you through configuring WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF, then applying AS_PATH and MED outbound. Finally, we'll highlight common mistakes such as route-map implicit deny and the risk of unintended reachability changes. By the end, you'll be able to define a clear policy for an outbound preference and craft inbound hints to your providers. Think about one traffic flow you need to prioritize in your network — this chapter will show you the exact BGP attributes and commands to do it.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › BGP Route Manipulation
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Route Manipulation & Path Control

Learn the attribute-level controls that let you prefer exits, discourage peers, and hint entry points. Practical configs with verification are provided so you can test safely in a lab.

In this lesson
  • How WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF affect outbound choices.
  • Using AS_PATH prepend and MED to influence inbound traffic.
  • Implementing policies with route-maps and prefix-lists, and verification steps.
Visual concept
R1 (AS65001)
ISP-A (AS65002)
ISP-B (AS65003)
Use WEIGHT on R1 to prefer one eBGP neighbor, LOCAL_PREF to prefer an exit across the AS, AS_PATH prepend to make a path less attractive externally, and MED to advise an adjacent AS where to enter.
Explore Key Topics
WEIGHT
Router-local, immediate control for outbound path selection.
LOCAL_PREF
AS-wide exit preference shared via iBGP.
AS_PATH / MED
Make paths less attractive externally or hint preferred entry points.

screens.title: Learning Objectives

You will also use route-maps and prefix-lists to match and modify BGP updates safely. We will make the important distinction between inbound and outbound BGP policies and when to apply them. Finally, you will design a simple BGP policy to meet a traffic engineering goal and verify it with show commands. Each objective emphasizes hands-on verification and safe testing in a lab. For example, you will configure a route-map that sets LOCAL_PREF on routes learned from ISP-A so that all routers in your AS prefer that exit. You will also practice AS_PATH prepending to influence how peers choose their entry. Throughout the lesson we stress common pitfalls, like the implicit deny at the end of route-maps, and safe verification steps such as clearing specific BGP updates and checking show ip bgp. These objectives prepare you to craft practical, testable policies in an enterprise environment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Lab
screens.narratorSegment: This lab-first objective set explains the practical steps you will take. You will begin by reviewing the BGP best path selection algorithm and then configure WEIGHT on a router to prefer one eBGP neighbor. Next you will configure LOCAL_PREF using a route-map applied inbound so that the preferred exit propagates across the AS. Then you'll practice AS_PATH prepending and MED on outbound advertisements to influence how remote peers enter your AS. Each step includes verification using show ip bgp and soft clears of specific prefixes to re-evaluate attributes. You will also complete a small assessment that matches attributes to their primary use cases. Emphasis will be on safe testing: make changes on lab routers only, verify the single prefix, and observe effects before applying wider automation. This objective prepares you to apply attribute changes with confidence and to reason about their scope and impact across your AS and neighboring ASes.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Learning Objectives — Lab
Lab Walkthrough Steps
  1. Review BGP best path attributes and decision order.
  2. Configure WEIGHT on R1 to prefer ISP-A for outbound traffic.
  3. Apply LOCAL_PREF via route-map inbound from ISP-A and verify propagation.
  4. Set AS_PATH prepend and MED outbound, then verify inbound behavior.
Verification Checklist
  • Use show ip bgp <prefix> to compare attributes.
  • Use clear ip bgp <prefix> soft in/out to re-evaluate.
  • Watch for implicit deny in route-maps and unexpected withdraws.

screens.title: What is BGP route manipulation?
screens.narratorSegment: BGP route manipulation is the deliberate modification of BGP path attributes to influence the best path selection process. The goal is traffic engineering — making the network send or receive traffic according to operational or business priorities. Manipulation changes how your routers and peers see prefixes by altering attributes such as WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, and MED. Use route manipulation when you need predictable exit points for outbound traffic, or when you need to encourage or discourage a peer from using a particular entry into your AS. It is not a substitute for capacity planning; rather, it gives you finer control over which links carry specific flows. A common example is preferring ISP-A for outbound internet traffic by setting LOCAL_PREF higher on routes learned from ISP-A, so all internal routers elect that exit. A typical misconception is thinking these changes are global when they are not: WEIGHT is strictly local to a router, LOCAL_PREF is propagated via iBGP, AS_PATH prepend is visible to external peers, and MED is just a hint to an adjacent AS. Always test in a lab and verify with show ip bgp before and after changes. How might changing one attribute affect routes you did not intend? That question guides cautious deployment.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › What is BGP route manipulation?
Definition

Change path attributes to influence routing

Route manipulation adjusts attributes that the BGP algorithm evaluates so you control preferred paths without changing topology.

When to use
When you need predictable exit points, avoid congested links, or signal preferred entries to peers.
Misconception
Altering one attribute can affect other prefixes; attribute scope matters — test in lab.
Concrete example
You want all routers in AS 65001 to prefer ISP-A. Rather than changing routes individually, set LOCAL_PREF higher on routes learned from ISP-A so every iBGP peer chooses that exit.
Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

Each BGP attribute affects path selection differently; choose the attribute whose scope matches your goal and verify changes carefully.

screens.title: WEIGHT — Router-local control
screens.narratorSegment: WEIGHT is a Cisco-proprietary attribute that is evaluated before most other attributes in the BGP decision process. It exists only on the local router, so setting a higher WEIGHT on R1 for neighbor ISP-A will make R1 prefer that path for outbound traffic from R1 itself. WEIGHT does not get shared to other routers; it is a local override. A concrete configuration example is to set neighbor 192.168.10.1 weight 200 and neighbor 192.168.20.1 weight 100, so R1 prefers ISP-A. Use WEIGHT when you need immediate, localized control — for instance, to prefer one uplink on a specific edge router handling local services. A common misconception is assuming WEIGHT will alter the entire AS's behavior; it will not. Also avoid heavy reliance on WEIGHT for distributed policy because it can produce inconsistent paths across routers. Verify the effect with show ip bgp on the router where weight was changed, and use targeted soft clears to re-evaluate only affected prefixes. In lab practice, document the initial best path, apply the weight, and confirm the router's decision changed as expected. WEIGHT — Router-local control means weight gives immediate local control over path selection on one router and is not propagated across the as.. In practical terms, how to prefer an ebgp neighbor on a single router. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › WEIGHT — Router-local control
What is WEIGHT?

Local attribute used to prefer a path

WEIGHT is evaluated early in the BGP decision process and affects only the router where it is configured.

Configuration example
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.10.1 remote-as 65002
 neighbor 192.168.10.1 weight 200    ! Prefer ISP-A locally
 neighbor 192.168.20.1 remote-as 65003
 neighbor 192.168.20.1 weight 100    ! Lower weight for ISP-B
Use case

Prefer one of two eBGP paths for outbound traffic originating from this router. Useful for edge routers offering local services.

Misconception
Do not expect WEIGHT to influence other routers; it does not propagate via BGP.
Key Takeaway

WEIGHT is the right tool for single-router outbound preference; use LOCAL_PREF when you need AS-wide behavior.

screens.title: LOCAL_PREF — AS-wide outbound preference
screens.narratorSegment: LOCAL_PREF is an attribute shared among iBGP peers to influence the preferred exit point for outbound traffic from the AS. A higher LOCAL_PREF is preferred and, when set on routes learned from an eBGP neighbor and applied inbound, that preference propagates to all routers within the AS. For example, setting local-preference 200 on routes received from ISP-A ensures every iBGP peer prefers ISP-A as the exit for those destinations. Configuration is typically done with a route-map that matches desired prefixes and then sets local-preference. One practical benefit is consistency: instead of configuring every router individually, LOCAL_PREF provides an AS-wide policy. A common error is applying the route-map in the wrong direction; to change your AS's exit, you apply the route-map inbound on the eBGP neighbor so the routes are received with the modified LOCAL_PREF. Verify propagation with show ip bgp on multiple routers to confirm they all see the higher LOCAL_PREF and choose the same exit. If propagation fails, check your iBGP mesh or route-reflector configuration. LOCAL_PREF — AS-wide outbound preference means local_pref sets an as-wide exit preference; configure via route-map inbound from ebgp peers for consistent behavior.. In practical terms, how local_pref shapes exit selection across an as. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: LOCAL_PREF sets an AS-wide exit preference; configure via route-map inbound from eBGP peers for consistent behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › LOCAL_PREF — AS-wide outbound preference
Purpose

Choose the preferred exit for the entire AS

LOCAL_PREF is shared between iBGP peers. Set it on routes learned from an eBGP neighbor to control AS-wide outbound behavior.

Config snippet
ip access-list standard ISP_A_ROUTES
 permit any
!
route-map SET_LOCAL_PREF_ISP_A permit 10
 match ip address ISP_A_ROUTES
 set local-preference 200
!
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 route-map SET_LOCAL_PREF_ISP_A in
Verification

Use show ip bgp <prefix> on several routers to ensure they all see the increased LOCAL_PREF and select the same exit.

Pitfall
Applying the route-map in the wrong direction won't change the AS exit. Apply it inbound on the eBGP neighbor.
Key Takeaway

LOCAL_PREF is the standard mechanism to steer AS-wide outbound traffic. Use route-maps inbound on eBGP peers and verify propagation.

screens.title: AS_PATH Prepending — Influence incoming paths
screens.narratorSegment: AS_PATH prepending makes your prefixes look less attractive to external peers by artificially lengthening the AS path that they see. Since external peers prefer shorter AS_PATHs, adding your AS number multiple times to routes you advertise makes those routes less likely to be chosen by remote networks. For example, adding set as-path prepend 65001 65001 65001 on routes sent to ISP-B will encourage other ASes to use ISP-A instead if ISP-A offers a shorter AS_PATH. This technique should be applied outbound to the eBGP neighbor whose routing decisions you want to influence. A common use case is steering inbound traffic so that a particular ISP or link receives most of the traffic to your prefixes. However, excessive prepending can make your prefixes unattractive and cause reachability problems if peers consistently avoid your AS. Always test with a limited prefix and verify via show ip bgp on your providers if possible. Remember: AS_PATH prepending is a tool to influence external routing behavior, not a guarantee. AS_PATH Prepending — Influence incoming paths means prepending lengthens the as_path seen by peers to make a route less preferred externally; apply outbound to the peer you want to discourage.. In practical terms, making your as_path look longer to discourage peers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AS_PATH in brief
keyIdea.text: Prepending lengthens the AS_PATH seen by peers to make a route less preferred externally; apply outbound to the peer you want to discourage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › AS_PATH Prepending
How it works

Prepending adds copies of your AS number to the AS_PATH you advertise so remote ASes prefer other, shorter paths.

Config example
ip access-list standard MY_NETWORKS
 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
!
route-map PREPEND_AS permit 10
 match ip address MY_NETWORKS
 set as-path prepend 65001 65001 65001
!
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.20.1 route-map PREPEND_AS out
Use case

Encourage an external AS to enter your network through a different provider or link by making this path less attractive.

Caution
Excessive prepending can cause peers to prefer paths that bypass your network or make your prefixes unreachable to some networks.
Key Takeaway

AS_PATH prepend is an outbound policy used to influence inbound traffic; treat it as a hint and test carefully.

screens.title: MED — Multi-Exit Discriminator
screens.narratorSegment: The Multi-Exit Discriminator, or MED, is an attribute you advertise to an adjacent AS to suggest which entry point they should use when multiple links connect your networks. A lower MED value is preferred by the neighbor. MED is not a universal rule across all ASes because the receiving AS may ignore MED or use other policies; therefore MED is a hint, not an absolute. Use MED when you want a neighbor to prefer a specific link to reach your prefixes — for example, set metric 20 outbound to ISP-A via link one so ISP-A prefers link one as the entry. MED is applied outbound to the eBGP peer that you want to influence. Common pitfalls include expecting MED to override a shorter AS_PATH on the neighbor's side; many networks prioritize AS_PATH before MED. Always coordinate with your upstream when relying on MED for critical traffic flows and verify the neighbor's behavior where possible. MED — Multi-Exit Discriminator means med hints an adjacent as about preferred entry; lower is preferred but it is only a hint and may be ignored.. In practical terms, hint to adjacent as about preferred entry point. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › MED — Multi-Exit Discriminator
What MED does

MED is an outbound hint to a neighboring AS about which entry point to prefer for your prefixes when multiple links exist.

Config example
ip access-list standard MY_NETWORKS
 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
!
route-map SET_MED_LOW permit 10
 match ip address MY_NETWORKS
 set metric 20
!
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.10.1 route-map SET_MED_LOW out
Practical note

MED is often vendor-specific in how it's compared. Many ASes prefer AS_PATH before MED, so MED should be used in coordination with the neighbor.

Misconception
MED will not always win against other attributes; treat it as a suggestion and verify behavior with upstream.
Key Takeaway

MED hints a preferred entry point to a neighbor, but its effectiveness depends on the neighbor's policy and attribute ordering.

screens.title: Prefix-lists and route-maps
screens.narratorSegment: Prefix-lists and route-maps are the primary tools for matching and modifying BGP updates. Prefix-lists are efficient and designed specifically for prefix matching. They allow exact matches or range matches using ge and le for mask-length flexibility. For example, ip prefix-list MY_PREFIXES seq 5 permit 10.0.0.0/24 will match that exact prefix; using ge and le lets you match subnet ranges. Route-maps are sequential policy containers composed of permit or deny statements. Each statement can match criteria such as prefix-list membership or as-path and then set attributes like local-preference or as-path prepend. A critical detail is that route-maps have an implicit deny any at the end. If a route does not match any permit statement it will be denied, which often surprises engineers who expect unmatched routes to be passed through. The safe pattern is to explicitly add a final permit statement to allow other routes or to structure deny/permit entries intentionally. Use prefix-lists for matching prefixes and route-maps for actions. Always test route-map logic in a lab and verify with show ip bgp and controlled advertisements. Prefix-lists and route-maps means use prefix-lists for efficient matching and route-maps for sequential match/set actions; always account for the implicit deny at the end of route-maps.. In practical terms, matching and modifying routes safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Prefix-lists and route-maps
Prefix-list examples
ip prefix-list MY_PREFIXES seq 5 permit 10.0.0.0/24
ip prefix-list MY_PREFIXES seq 10 permit 172.16.0.0/22 ge 24 le 26

Use ge and le to match variable mask lengths within a range. Prefix-lists are more efficient than generic ACLs for routing policy.

Route-map pattern
route-map EXAMPLE permit 10
 match ip address prefix-list MY_PREFIXES
 set local-preference 200
route-map EXAMPLE permit 20  ! permit everything else

Remember the implicit deny at the end of a route-map. Add an explicit permit if you intend to allow other routes unchanged.

Common pitfall

A route-map that only matches a subset of prefixes without a final permit will implicitly deny all other routes. Explicitly permit if needed.

screens.title: Inbound vs Outbound Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the direction of a route-map is essential to achieving the intended effect. An inbound policy (neighbor route-map in) is applied to routes received from a neighbor. Use inbound policies to influence how your AS perceives external routes and to set attributes like LOCAL_PREF or WEIGHT on received prefixes. An outbound policy (neighbor route-map out) is applied to routes you advertise to a neighbor. Use outbound policies to change how the neighbor sees your prefixes — for example, AS_PATH prepend or MED. A common mistake is applying a LOCAL_PREF change outbound to a neighbor; that does not change how your AS sees the route. Another trap is applying an AS_PATH prepend inbound — since prepending affects the AS_PATH you advertise, it must be outbound. In practice, begin by asking whether you want to change your own AS's decisions or influence a neighbor's choices. If it's your AS's decision, modify inbound attributes. If it's the neighbor's view of your routes, modify outbound advertisements. Always verify with show ip bgp before and after and use targeted soft clears when available to re-evaluate paths.

keyIdea.text: Inbound policies affect your AS's perception; outbound policies affect how neighbors perceive your routes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Inbound vs Outbound Policies
Inbound (route-map in)

Applied to routes received from a neighbor. Use to set WEIGHT or LOCAL_PREF so your AS prefers a specific exit.

Example question
You want all routers in AS 65001 to prefer ISP-A. Apply a LOCAL_PREF route-map inbound from ISP-A so the attribute propagates via iBGP.
Outbound (route-map out)

Applied to routes you send to a neighbor. Use it to set AS_PATH prepend or MED so the neighbor and their peers see altered attributes.

Common mistake
Applying AS_PATH prepend on the wrong direction means the neighbor never sees the change. Prepend must be outbound.
Quick checklist
If you want to influence your AS's exit, apply route-maps inbound on eBGP peers. If you want to influence how a neighbor reaches you, apply route-maps outbound to that neighbor.

screens.title: Lab: Configure and verify WEIGHT
screens.narratorSegment: In this step you will configure WEIGHT on a router to prefer ISP-A for outbound traffic from that router. screens.title: Lab: Configure LOCAL_PREF with a route-map
screens.narratorSegment: This lab step configures LOCAL_PREF so that all routers in AS 65001 prefer ISP-A for outbound internet traffic. Begin by defining a prefix-list or access-list that matches the test prefixes, then create a route-map that sets local-preference 200 for those matches. Apply the route-map inbound on the eBGP neighbor connected to ISP-A. Example: create ip prefix-list ISP_A_ROUTES permit 203.0.113.0/24, then route-map PREFER_ISP_A permit 10 match ip address prefix-list ISP_A_ROUTES set local-preference 200, and finally neighbor 192.168.12.2 route-map PREFER_ISP_A in under router bgp. After configuring, soft clear the prefix and use show ip bgp on your internal routers to check that they see LOCAL_PREF 200 and choose ISP-A. This change propagates via iBGP so check more than one router to confirm AS-wide behavior. A misconception to avoid is only checking the router where you applied the route-map; LOCAL_PREF's effect is intentionally wider. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential points to carry forward. WEIGHT controls path choice on a single router and is not propagated; use it for local overrides. LOCAL_PREF controls AS-wide exit selection and is set on routes learned inbound from eBGP neighbors so iBGP peers prefer that exit. AS_PATH prepending lengthens the AS_PATH you advertise and discourages remote ASes from selecting that path; apply it outbound to the neighbor you want to influence. MED is a hint to an adjacent AS about which link to use to reach your prefixes; lower MED is preferred but many ASes treat it as secondary to other attributes. Use prefix-lists for efficient prefix matching and route-maps for sequential match-and-set policies. Always remember route-maps have an implicit deny — add explicit permits when you need to allow unmatched routes. Finally, always test changes in a lab, verify with show ip bgp and targeted soft clears, and coordinate with providers when using MED and prepending. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to shape traffic at the BGP layer by changing path attributes. These attributes let you influence the BGP best path algorithm so your network sends or receives traffic where you intend. We will cover four primary knobs — WEIGHT for router-local decisions; LOCAL_PREF for AS-wide outbound preference; AS_PATH prepending to discourage external peers; and MED to hint preferred entry points for an adjacent AS. You'll also learn how to implement these changes safely with route-maps and prefix-lists, how to apply them in the correct direction, and how to verify results with show commands. Practical examples and a step-by-step lab will walk you through configuring WEIGHT and LOCAL_PREF, then applying AS_PATH and MED outbound. Finally, we'll highlight common mistakes such as route-map implicit deny and the risk of unintended reachability changes. By the end, you'll be able to define a clear policy for an outbound preference and craft inbound hints to your providers. Think about one traffic flow you need to prioritize in your network — this chapter will show you the exact BGP attributes and commands to do it.

By the end of this chapter you will implement route manipulation techniques using WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH prepend, and MED. You will also use route-maps and prefix-lists to match and modify BGP updates safely. We will make the important distinction between inbound and outbound BGP policies and when to apply them. Finally, you will design a simple BGP policy to meet a traffic engineering goal and verify it with show commands. Each objective emphasizes hands-on verification and safe testing in a lab. For example, you will configure a route-map that sets LOCAL_PREF on routes learned from ISP-A so that all routers in your AS prefer that exit. You will also practice AS_PATH prepending to influence how peers choose their entry. Throughout the lesson we stress common pitfalls, like the implicit deny at the end of route-maps, and safe verification steps such as clearing specific BGP updates and checking show ip bgp. These objectives prepare you to craft practical, testable policies in an enterprise environment.

This lab-first objective set explains the practical steps you will take. You will begin by reviewing the BGP best path selection algorithm and then configure WEIGHT on a router to prefer one eBGP neighbor. Next you will configure LOCAL_PREF using a route-map applied inbound so that the preferred exit propagates across the AS. Then you'll practice AS_PATH prepending and MED on outbound advertisements to influence how remote peers enter your AS. Each step includes verification using show ip bgp and soft clears of specific prefixes to re-evaluate attributes. You will also complete a small assessment that matches attributes to their primary use cases. Emphasis will be on safe testing: make changes on lab routers only, verify the single prefix, and observe effects before applying wider automation. This objective prepares you to apply attribute changes with confidence and to reason about their scope and impact across your AS and neighboring ASes.

BGP route manipulation is the deliberate modification of BGP path attributes to influence the best path selection process. The goal is traffic engineering — making the network send or receive traffic according to operational or business priorities. Manipulation changes how your routers and peers see prefixes by altering attributes such as WEIGHT, LOCAL_PREF, AS_PATH, and MED. Use route manipulation when you need predictable exit points for outbound traffic, or when you need to encourage or discourage a peer from using a particular entry into your AS. It is not a substitute for capacity planning; rather, it gives you finer control over which links carry specific flows. A common example is preferring ISP-A for outbound internet traffic by setting LOCAL_PREF higher on routes learned from ISP-A, so all internal routers elect that exit. A typical misconception is thinking these changes are global when they are not: WEIGHT is strictly local to a router, LOCAL_PREF is propagated via iBGP, AS_PATH prepend is visible to external peers, and MED is just a hint to an adjacent AS. Always test in a lab and verify with show ip bgp before and after changes. How might changing one attribute affect routes you did not intend? That question guides cautious deployment.

WEIGHT is a Cisco-proprietary attribute that is evaluated before most other attributes in the BGP decision process. It exists only on the local router, so setting a higher WEIGHT on R1 for neighbor ISP-A will make R1 prefer that path for outbound traffic from R1 itself. WEIGHT does not get shared to other routers; it is a local override. A concrete configuration example is to set neighbor 192.168.10.1 weight 200 and neighbor 192.168.20.1 weight 100, so R1 prefers ISP-A. Use WEIGHT when you need immediate, localized control — for instance, to prefer one uplink on a specific edge router handling local services. A common misconception is assuming WEIGHT will alter the entire AS's behavior; it will not. Also avoid heavy reliance on WEIGHT for distributed policy because it can produce inconsistent paths across routers. Verify the effect with show ip bgp on the router where weight was changed, and use targeted soft clears to re-evaluate only affected prefixes. LOCAL_PREF is an attribute shared among iBGP peers to influence the preferred exit point for outbound traffic from the AS. A higher LOCAL_PREF is preferred and, when set on routes learned from an eBGP neighbor and applied inbound, that preference propagates to all routers within the AS. For example, setting local-preference 200 on routes received from ISP-A ensures every iBGP peer prefers ISP-A as the exit for those destinations. Configuration is typically done with a route-map that matches desired prefixes and then sets local-preference. One practical benefit is consistency: instead of configuring every router individually, LOCAL_PREF provides an AS-wide policy. A common error is applying the route-map in the wrong direction; to change your AS's exit, you apply the route-map inbound on the eBGP neighbor so the routes are received with the modified LOCAL_PREF. Verify propagation with show ip bgp on multiple routers to confirm they all see the higher LOCAL_PREF and choose the same exit. If propagation fails, check your iBGP mesh or route-reflector configuration. AS_PATH prepending makes your prefixes look less attractive to external peers by artificially lengthening the AS path that they see. Since external peers prefer shorter AS_PATHs, adding your AS number multiple times to routes you advertise makes those routes less likely to be chosen by remote networks. For example, adding set as-path prepend 65001 65001 65001 on routes sent to ISP-B will encourage other ASes to use ISP-A instead if ISP-A offers a shorter AS_PATH. This technique should be applied outbound to the eBGP neighbor whose routing decisions you want to influence. A common use case is steering inbound traffic so that a particular ISP or link receives most of the traffic to your prefixes. However, excessive prepending can make your prefixes unattractive and cause reachability problems if peers consistently avoid your AS. Always test with a limited prefix and verify via show ip bgp on your providers if possible. Remember: AS_PATH prepending is a tool to influence external routing behavior, not a guarantee. The Multi-Exit Discriminator, or MED, is an attribute you advertise to an adjacent AS to suggest which entry point they should use when multiple links connect your networks. A lower MED value is preferred by the neighbor. MED is not a universal rule across all ASes because the receiving AS may ignore MED or use other policies; therefore MED is a hint, not an absolute. Use MED when you want a neighbor to prefer a specific link to reach your prefixes — for example, set metric 20 outbound to ISP-A via link one so ISP-A prefers link one as the entry. MED is applied outbound to the eBGP peer that you want to influence. Common pitfalls include expecting MED to override a shorter AS_PATH on the neighbor's side; many networks prioritize AS_PATH before MED. Always coordinate with your upstream when relying on MED for critical traffic flows and verify the neighbor's behavior where possible. Prefix-lists and route-maps are the primary tools for matching and modifying BGP updates. Prefix-lists are efficient and designed specifically for prefix matching. They allow exact matches or range matches using ge and le for mask-length flexibility. For example, ip prefix-list MY_PREFIXES seq 5 permit 10.0.0.0/24 will match that exact prefix; using ge and le lets you match subnet ranges. Route-maps are sequential policy containers composed of permit or deny statements. Each statement can match criteria such as prefix-list membership or as-path and then set attributes like local-preference or as-path prepend. A critical detail is that route-maps have an implicit deny any at the end. If a route does not match any permit statement it will be denied, which often surprises engineers who expect unmatched routes to be passed through. The safe pattern is to explicitly add a final permit statement to allow other routes or to structure deny/permit entries intentionally. Use prefix-lists for matching prefixes and route-maps for actions. Always test route-map logic in a lab and verify with show ip bgp and controlled advertisements. Understanding the direction of a route-map is essential to achieving the intended effect. An inbound policy (neighbor route-map in) is applied to routes received from a neighbor. Use inbound policies to influence how your AS perceives external routes and to set attributes like LOCAL_PREF or WEIGHT on received prefixes. An outbound policy (neighbor route-map out) is applied to routes you advertise to a neighbor. Use outbound policies to change how the neighbor sees your prefixes — for example, AS_PATH prepend or MED. A common mistake is applying a LOCAL_PREF change outbound to a neighbor; that does not change how your AS sees the route. Another trap is applying an AS_PATH prepend inbound — since prepending affects the AS_PATH you advertise, it must be outbound. In practice, begin by asking whether you want to change your own AS's decisions or influence a neighbor's choices. If it's your AS's decision, modify inbound attributes. If it's the neighbor's view of your routes, modify outbound advertisements. Always verify with show ip bgp before and after and use targeted soft clears when available to re-evaluate paths.

These are the essential points to carry forward. WEIGHT controls path choice on a single router and is not propagated; use it for local overrides. LOCAL_PREF controls AS-wide exit selection and is set on routes learned inbound from eBGP neighbors so iBGP peers prefer that exit. AS_PATH prepending lengthens the AS_PATH you advertise and discourages remote ASes from selecting that path; apply it outbound to the neighbor you want to influence. MED is a hint to an adjacent AS about which link to use to reach your prefixes; lower MED is preferred but many ASes treat it as secondary to other attributes. Use prefix-lists for efficient prefix matching and route-maps for sequential match-and-set policies. Always remember route-maps have an implicit deny — add explicit permits when you need to allow unmatched routes. Finally, always test changes in a lab, verify with show ip bgp and targeted soft clears, and coordinate with providers when using MED and prepending. Keep three compact rules in mind as you apply route manipulation. First, pick the attribute with the correct scope: WEIGHT for single-router decisions, LOCAL_PREF for AS-wide exit choice, and AS_PATH or MED to influence external peers. Second, pay attention to policy direction: to change how your AS exits choose inbound route-maps; to change how a neighbor views your prefixes choose outbound route-maps. Third, always test changes on a small set of prefixes and verify with show ip bgp and soft clears. Also remember the implicit deny at the end of route-maps which can silently block routes. Following these rules will reduce risk and make your traffic engineering predictable. Which of these rules would you rehearse first in a lab? Try it on a single prefix and observe the results.
